For baseball, set the app up as a **ruleset-driven model**: one core baseball database, then separate configuration layers for **MLB**, **NPB/KBO/CPBL/ABL**, and **international tournaments** such as the World Baseball Classic, Premier12 and Olympics-style WBSC events.

Baseball is one of the best sports for analytics because almost every action is discrete: pitch → swing/take/contact → batted ball/fielding event → base/out state → run expectancy change. The biggest mistake would be only tracking ERA, batting average and recent wins. A strong baseball app needs **pitch-level data, batter-vs-pitcher matchups, park effects, weather, bullpen availability, umpire tendencies, handedness, lineup quality, defensive quality and rule-specific constraints**.

## 1. Core baseball data structure

### A. Match metadata

| Category       | Necessary fields                                                                   |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Competition    | MLB, NPB, KBO, CPBL, ABL, WBC, Premier12, Olympics, domestic league                |
| Match          | game ID, date, local start time, timezone, venue, home/away/neutral                |
| Series context | regular season, playoffs, group stage, knockout, doubleheader, series game 1/2/3/4 |
| Ruleset        | innings, DH rule, extra-innings rule, mercy rule, pitch clock, roster limits       |
| Teams          | team IDs, managers, confirmed/probable lineups, probable pitchers                  |
| Game state     | inning, half-inning, outs, score, runners on base, pitch count, leverage           |
| Travel/rest    | days rest, road trip length, time-zone shift, doubleheader fatigue                 |
| Weather        | temperature, wind, humidity, rain risk, roof status, air density                   |
| Park           | dimensions, altitude, wall height, foul territory, park factor                     |
| Officials      | plate umpire, base umpires, replay crew, strike-zone tendency                      |

Statcast/MLB-style data is the elite reference point for baseball apps because it captures pitch tracking, batted-ball quality, fielding, baserunning, expected stats and park effects. Baseball Savant’s Statcast leaderboards include expected statistics, fielding, baserunning, arm strength, sprint speed and other measured data. ([MLB.com][1])

## 2. Pitch-by-pitch event table

This should be the heart of your baseball app.

| Field             | Example                                                               |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| game_id           | unique game                                                           |
| inning            | 1–9+                                                                  |
| half_inning       | top/bottom                                                            |
| outs              | 0, 1, 2                                                               |
| batting_team_id   | offence                                                               |
| fielding_team_id  | defence                                                               |
| pitcher_id        | current pitcher                                                       |
| batter_id         | hitter                                                                |
| catcher_id        | catcher                                                               |
| pitcher_hand      | R/L                                                                   |
| batter_hand       | R/L/S                                                                 |
| count             | 0-0, 1-2, 3-2                                                         |
| runners_on        | empty, 1B, 2B, 3B, combinations                                       |
| pitch_number_game | global pitch count                                                    |
| pitch_number_pa   | pitch within plate appearance                                         |
| pitch_type        | four-seam, sinker, cutter, slider, sweeper, curve, changeup, splitter |
| pitch_velocity    | mph/km/h                                                              |
| pitch_spin_rate   | rpm                                                                   |
| pitch_movement    | horizontal/vertical break                                             |
| release_point     | x/y/z release coordinates                                             |
| extension         | pitcher extension                                                     |
| location          | plate x/z                                                             |
| intended_location | catcher target if available                                           |
| result            | ball, called strike, swinging strike, foul, in play                   |
| contact_type      | groundball, line drive, flyball, popup                                |
| exit_velocity     | mph/km/h                                                              |
| launch_angle      | degrees                                                               |
| spray_angle       | pull/centre/oppo                                                      |
| hit_distance      | projected distance                                                    |
| expected_stats    | xBA, xSLG, xwOBA                                                      |
| run_value         | pitch/PA run value                                                    |
| win_probability   | before/after                                                          |
| leverage_index    | low/medium/high                                                       |
| umpire_call       | called ball/strike, correct/incorrect if tracking available           |
| video_link        | optional clip                                                         |
| source            | Statcast/API/manual/video                                             |
| confidence        | verified/estimated                                                    |

MLB’s expected-stat framework uses batted-ball quality such as exit velocity and launch angle; Baseball Savant describes xwOBA as being formulated from exit velocity, launch angle and, for some batted balls, sprint speed. ([baseballsavant.com][2]) Barrels are also a key batted-ball-quality metric; MLB defines a Barrel as requiring at least 98 mph exit velocity, with qualifying launch-angle ranges widening as exit velocity increases. ([MLB.com][3])

## 3. Player-level stats

## A. Hitter stats

### Traditional hitter stats

| Category   | Stats                                                               |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Basic      | games, plate appearances, at-bats, runs, hits, doubles, triples, HR |
| Rate stats | AVG, OBP, SLG, OPS                                                  |
| Production | RBI, runs created, total bases                                      |
| Discipline | walks, strikeouts, BB%, K%, BB/K                                    |
| Contact    | contact %, swinging-strike %, called-strike %, chase rate           |
| Power      | isolated power, HR/FB, extra-base-hit rate                          |
| Splits     | vs RHP, vs LHP, home/away, day/night, grass/turf                    |
| Form       | last 7/14/30 days, last 5/10/20 games                               |

### Advanced hitter stats

| Category           | Stats                                                           |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Quality of contact | exit velocity, hard-hit %, barrel %, sweet-spot %, launch angle |
| Expected stats     | xBA, xSLG, xwOBA, xwOBAcon                                      |
| Plate discipline   | chase %, zone contact %, whiff %, swing %, first-pitch swing %  |
| Pitch-type splits  | vs fastball, breaking ball, off-speed, sinker, slider, sweeper  |
| Count splits       | ahead, behind, two-strike, full count                           |
| Handedness         | batter vs pitcher handedness, platoon advantage                 |
| Situational        | RISP, bases loaded, two outs, late/close, high leverage         |
| Baserunning        | sprint speed, stolen bases, caught stealing, extra bases taken  |
| Value              | wRC+, WAR, batting runs, WPA, RE24                              |

wRC+ is especially important because it adjusts offensive production for league and park context; FanGraphs defines 100 as league average, with every point above or below representing a percentage point better or worse than average. ([Sabermetrics Library][4])

## B. Pitcher stats

### Traditional pitcher stats

| Category          | Stats                                                         |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Workload          | games, starts, innings pitched, batters faced, pitches thrown |
| Results           | wins, losses, saves, holds, blown saves                       |
| Run prevention    | ERA, runs allowed, earned runs, WHIP                          |
| Strikeout/control | strikeouts, walks, K/9, BB/9, K/BB                            |
| Contact allowed   | hits allowed, HR allowed, extra-base hits allowed             |
| Splits            | vs RHB/LHB, home/away, day/night                              |
| Form              | last 3/5/10 starts or appearances                             |

### Advanced pitcher stats

| Category             | Stats                                                           |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Fielding-independent | FIP, xFIP, SIERA-style indicators                               |
| Strikeout skill      | K%, swinging-strike %, CSW%, called-strike %, chase induced     |
| Control              | BB%, zone %, first-pitch strike %, waste-pitch rate             |
| Contact management   | hard-hit %, barrel %, average EV allowed, launch angle allowed  |
| Expected results     | xERA, xwOBA allowed, xBA allowed, xSLG allowed                  |
| Pitch arsenal        | pitch mix %, velocity, spin, movement, release point, extension |
| Pitch value          | run value by pitch, whiff by pitch, chase by pitch              |
| Times through order  | 1st/2nd/3rd time through lineup splits                          |
| Workload/fatigue     | pitch count, days rest, velocity drop, injury history           |
| Bullpen role         | opener, bulk reliever, setup, closer, long relief               |

FIP is useful because it focuses on outcomes more directly controlled by pitchers, while xFIP regresses home-run rate toward expected levels using fly balls and league-average HR/FB assumptions. ([Sabermetrics Library][5])

## C. Catcher stats

| Category        | Stats                                                             |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Receiving       | framing runs, called strikes gained/lost, low-zone skill          |
| Blocking        | blocks, passed balls, wild pitches blocked, blocking runs         |
| Throwing        | pop time, arm strength, caught stealing %, pickoff attempts       |
| Game calling    | pitcher ERA/FIP with catcher, pitch sequencing, target setup      |
| Workload        | games caught, innings caught, day-game-after-night-game fatigue   |
| Batter value    | OBP, SLG, wRC+, platoon splits                                    |
| Defensive value | catcher fielding run value, catcher ERA caveat, staff familiarity |

Statcast includes fielding/catching measures such as pop time, arm strength, lead distance and broader Fielding Run Value, which converts measurable defensive performance into a run-based scale. ([baseballsavant.com][6])

## D. Fielding stats

| Category            | Stats                                               |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Basic               | errors, assists, putouts, double plays              |
| Range               | outs above average, range factor, reaction/jump     |
| Arm                 | arm strength, throw accuracy, outfield assists      |
| Position-specific   | infield OAA, outfield OAA, catcher framing/blocking |
| Batted-ball context | fielding by groundball/liner/flyball/popup          |
| Shift/positioning   | starting position, alignment, depth                 |
| Value               | defensive runs saved, OAA, fielding run value       |

MLB’s Statcast glossary defines Outs Above Average as a range-based defensive metric showing how many outs a fielder saved relative to peers, and it now covers both outfielders and infielders. ([MLB.com][1])

## E. Baserunning stats

| Category    | Stats                                              |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Speed       | sprint speed, home-to-first, first-to-third speed  |
| Stealing    | stolen bases, caught stealing, success %, attempts |
| Leads/jumps | lead distance, secondary lead, steal jump          |
| Aggression  | extra bases taken, advancement on balls in play    |
| Mistakes    | pickoffs, outs on bases, failed advances           |
| Value       | baserunning runs, stolen-base run value, WPA added |

Statcast defines sprint speed as a player’s fastest one-second running window, and a “Bolt” as a run of at least 30 ft/sec. ([baseballsavant.com][7])

## 4. Team-level stats

## A. Team offence

| Category     | Stats                                                       |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Run scoring  | runs/game, wRC+, OPS, OBP, SLG                              |
| Power        | HR, ISO, barrel %, hard-hit %, extra-base-hit rate          |
| Discipline   | BB%, K%, chase %, contact %, pitches per PA                 |
| Situational  | RISP, bases loaded, high leverage, late/close               |
| Handedness   | vs RHP, vs LHP, platoon balance                             |
| Lineup depth | top 3, middle order, bottom 3, bench bats                   |
| Recent form  | last 7/14/30 days, last 5/10/20 games                       |
| Matchup      | offence vs starter arsenal, bullpen handedness, park factor |

## B. Team pitching

| Category  | Stats                                                       |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Starters  | ERA, FIP, xFIP, K%, BB%, xwOBA allowed                      |
| Bullpen   | ERA, FIP, leverage arms, closer availability                |
| Depth     | long relievers, lefty/righty mix, minor-league call-up risk |
| Workload  | pitches last 1/3/5 days, back-to-back appearances           |
| Platoon   | vs RHB/LHB, specialist relievers                            |
| Pitch mix | fastball-heavy, breaking-ball-heavy, groundball staff       |
| Fatigue   | bullpen overuse, starter short outings, travel schedule     |

## C. Team defence

| Category  | Stats                                                          |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Overall   | OAA, Defensive Runs Saved-style metrics, fielding run value    |
| Infield   | groundball conversion, double-play conversion, throwing errors |
| Outfield  | catch probability, arm strength, range, wall familiarity       |
| Catching  | framing, blocking, running-game control                        |
| Alignment | shift tendency, depth, no-doubles defence                      |
| Mistakes  | errors, unearned runs, missed cutoffs, passed balls            |

## D. Team game management

| Category            | Stats                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Manager tendencies  | bullpen hook speed, platoon substitutions, pinch-hitting |
| Bullpen usage       | closer usage, leverage matching, lefty/righty matchups   |
| Base running        | steal aggressiveness, sacrifice bunts, hit-and-run       |
| Defence             | late defensive substitutions, catcher swaps              |
| Lineup construction | stack handedness, protection, rest days                  |
| Challenge/replay    | replay challenge success, manager challenge tendency     |

## 5. Officials and umpire data

| Umpire feature                | Stats to capture                                                     |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Plate umpire                  | name, experience, historical strike-zone profile                     |
| Strike zone                   | called-strike rate, high/low/inside/outside tendencies               |
| Pitcher/batter effect         | favours pitchers, favours hitters, expands zone in two-strike counts |
| Walk/K impact                 | BB rate and K rate in games behind plate                             |
| Run environment               | average total runs with umpire, but adjust for teams/parks           |
| Ejections                     | ejection tendency, warnings, bench-clearing history                  |
| Replay crew                   | replay overturn rate, review speed                                   |
| Postseason/international crew | neutrality, experience, ruleset familiarity                          |

For MLB-specific modelling, umpire data is especially important because pitch location and called-strike tendencies directly change plate discipline, strikeouts, walks and pitch counts. For future MLB versions, also track ABS/challenge-system context separately; MLB has tested Automated Ball-Strike systems in the minors, and recent research notes the implementation has required complex operational choices rather than being a simple “rule to technology” translation. ([arXiv][8])

## 6. Venue, park and weather stats

| Category           | Necessary fields                                                  |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Park dimensions    | LF/LCF/CF/RCF/RF distance, wall height, foul territory            |
| Park factor        | runs, HR, doubles, triples, strikeouts, walks, handedness splits  |
| Altitude           | elevation, air density, ball carry                                |
| Roof               | open, closed, retractable, dome                                   |
| Surface            | grass/turf, speed, drainage                                       |
| Wind               | speed, direction, out to centre, in from outfield, crosswind      |
| Temperature        | game-time temp, hourly temp, heat effect                          |
| Humidity           | humidity, dew point, air density                                  |
| Rain               | delay risk, postponed risk, wet ball, bullpen disruption          |
| Sun/shadow         | batter visibility, day-game shadows, roof shadows                 |
| Historical scoring | average runs, HR, run suppression, bullpen/foul-territory effects |

Statcast park factors set 100 as average and compare how often events happen in a selected park versus the same players’ performance in other parks, controlled by handedness. ([baseballsavant.com][9]) Statcast also has venue-level factors for batted-ball speed/angle and environmental park factors, which makes park modelling more detailed than just “hitter’s park” or “pitcher’s park.” ([baseballsavant.com][10])

## 7. Match-state and prediction features

| Feature             | Why it matters                                        |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Base-out state      | run expectancy depends heavily on runners/outs        |
| Count               | 0-2 vs 3-1 changes batter/pitcher behaviour           |
| Inning              | bullpen leverage, closer availability, pinch-hit risk |
| Score differential  | changes steal/bunt/bullpen decisions                  |
| Leverage index      | high-leverage events are more valuable                |
| Pitch count         | starter fatigue and removal probability               |
| Times through order | starter penalty, lineup familiarity                   |
| Bullpen rest        | late-game win probability and totals                  |
| Platoon advantage   | R/L batter-pitcher matchups                           |
| Park/weather        | HR probability and run scoring                        |
| Umpire zone         | walk/K/run environment                                |
| Defensive strength  | BABIP, extra-base prevention, pitcher support         |

## 8. Derived advanced metrics

| Metric type             | Examples                                                             |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hitting value           | wRC+, xwOBA, xBA, xSLG, barrel %, hard-hit %                         |
| Pitching value          | FIP, xFIP, xERA, xwOBA allowed, CSW%, Stuff+/Pitching+ style metrics |
| Fielding value          | OAA, Fielding Run Value, catch probability, arm strength             |
| Baserunning value       | sprint speed, steal value, extra bases taken, runs above average     |
| Game state              | run expectancy, win probability, leverage index                      |
| Pitch value             | run value by pitch type, location value, arsenal quality             |
| Lineup quality          | projected wRC+ by batting slot, handedness balance                   |
| Bullpen quality         | available reliever index, fatigue-adjusted bullpen strength          |
| Park/weather adjustment | HR factor, run factor, air-density effect, wind effect               |
| Umpire adjustment       | strike-zone expansion, walk/K adjustment                             |
| Manager adjustment      | bullpen hook, pinch-hit tendency, defensive replacement tendency     |

## 10. MLB-specific layer

MLB should get its own layer because it has the richest public tracking data, Statcast metrics, specific rules, 162-game schedule dynamics, advanced park factors and deep bullpen/roster management.

### A. MLB-specific match context

| Category         | MLB-specific fields                                                     |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Schedule         | 162-game grind, series position, getaway day, doubleheader              |
| Roster           | 26-man roster, 40-man roster, options, call-ups, IL status              |
| Starting pitcher | probable starter, opener risk, pitch count expectation                  |
| Bullpen          | back-to-back usage, 3-in-4 usage, closer availability                   |
| Rules            | pitch clock, disengagement limits, shift restrictions, bigger bases     |
| Travel           | coast-to-coast road trips, time-zone changes, day game after night game |
| Park             | Statcast park factors, roof, altitude, wall dimensions                  |
| Deadline context | trade deadline buyers/sellers, September call-ups                       |
| Postseason       | Wild Card/Division/Championship/World Series roster usage               |

MLB’s 2023 rule changes introduced pitch timers, larger bases and defensive-shift restrictions; these should be versioned into the app because they affect pace, stolen-base environment, infield positioning and pitcher/batter timing. ([MLB.com][11])

### B. MLB-specific player stats

| Area     | Stats                                                                              |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hitters  | xwOBA, xBA, xSLG, barrel %, hard-hit %, chase %, whiff %, zone contact             |
| Pitchers | pitch velocity, spin rate, movement, extension, release point, xERA, xwOBA allowed |
| Fielders | OAA, Fielding Run Value, arm strength, route/jump, catch probability               |
| Catchers | pop time, framing, blocking, throwing, catcher defensive value                     |
| Runners  | sprint speed, bolts, lead distance, extra-base taken rate                          |
| Roster   | IL status, minor-league option status, call-up/fatigue context                     |

### C. MLB prediction feature weighting

| Feature group                        |  Importance |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------: |
| Starting pitcher quality and matchup |   Very high |
| Bullpen availability/fatigue         |   Very high |
| Lineup quality and handedness        |   Very high |
| Park/weather run environment         |   Very high |
| Batter-pitcher pitch-type matchup    |        High |
| Recent hitter contact quality        |        High |
| Umpire strike zone                   | Medium-high |
| Defence/catcher value                | Medium-high |
| Travel/rest/schedule spot            | Medium-high |
| Recent win-loss form                 |      Medium |
| Head-to-head                         |  Low-medium |

For MLB predictions, the biggest edge usually comes from combining **starter projection + bullpen fatigue + lineup handedness + park/weather + umpire zone**, rather than just ERA, batting average and team form.

## 11. International baseball layer

International baseball needs a separate layer because tournaments often have **short samples, uneven roster depth, pitch limits, national-team availability issues, mercy rules, different tie-breakers, and unfamiliar pitcher/batter matchups**.

This includes:

* World Baseball Classic;
* WBSC Premier12;
* Olympic-style tournaments;
* Asian Games;
* international friendlies;
* national-team qualifiers;
* underage tournaments;
* Caribbean Series-type events depending on scope.

WBSC is recognised by the International Olympic Committee as the global authority for baseball and softball, so WBSC event rules and competition manuals should be the baseline for non-MLB international rulesets. ([WBSC][12])

### A. International-specific match context

| Category         | Necessary fields                                                           |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tournament       | WBC, Premier12, qualifier, Olympics-style event                            |
| Stage            | group stage, quarterfinal, semifinal, final, placement game                |
| Roster rules     | player eligibility, MLB club restrictions, pitch limits                    |
| Pitch limits     | max pitches by stage, mandatory rest after pitch thresholds                |
| Mercy rules      | run-rule threshold by inning/stage                                         |
| Tie-breakers     | head-to-head, runs allowed/out, earned runs/out, batting average, lot draw |
| National roster  | MLB players, NPB/KBO/CPBL players, domestic league players                 |
| Availability     | club restrictions, insurance, travel, fatigue, spring-training timing      |
| Pitcher usage    | conservative usage, no overuse, short leash                                |
| Team chemistry   | national-team continuity, warm-up games, shared experience                 |
| Unknown matchups | limited batter-vs-pitcher history, scouting uncertainty                    |
| Neutral venue    | park familiarity, crowd support, travel distance                           |

For the 2026 World Baseball Classic, MLB’s rules page lists pitcher-use restrictions, including mandatory rest if a pitcher threw 30+ or 50+ pitches in the previous outing. ([MLB.com][13]) WBC pitch-count limits are stage-specific, with commonly reported caps of 65 pitches in the first round, 80 in quarterfinals, and 95 in semifinals/final, while pitchers may exceed the cap to finish a plate appearance. ([NBC 6 South Florida][14])

### B. International roster/player stats

| Category             | Stats                                                        |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Player source league | MLB, MiLB, NPB, KBO, CPBL, ABL, domestic, college            |
| Translation factor   | league-strength adjustment, park adjustment, run environment |
| Recent activity      | in-season, offseason, spring training, winter ball           |
| National-team form   | prior WBC/Premier12/qualifier performance                    |
| Role certainty       | MLB starter vs national-team role change                     |
| Pitcher restrictions | club-imposed cap, tournament cap, recent workload            |
| Chemistry            | catcher-pitcher familiarity, national-team continuity        |
| Travel adaptation    | jet lag, climate adaptation, venue familiarity               |
| Scouting gap         | limited data, unknown pitch mix, small-sample warning        |

### C. International team stats

| Category                 | Stats                                                            |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Roster strength          | MLB/NPB/KBO-level players, domestic depth                        |
| Pitching depth           | number of usable starters, bullpen depth, left/right balance     |
| Offensive depth          | top-order quality, bottom-order weakness, platoon balance        |
| Defence                  | catcher quality, infield defence, outfield arms                  |
| Style                    | small ball, power hitting, aggressive baserunning, bullpen-heavy |
| Tournament form          | warm-up games, group-stage results, run differential             |
| Pitch-limit resilience   | ability to cover innings under caps                              |
| Experience               | prior WBC/Premier12 success, knockout experience                 |
| Country-specific context | travel support, crowd, preparation window                        |

### D. International prediction feature weighting

| Feature group                            |  Importance |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------: |
| Pitching depth under pitch limits        |   Very high |
| Roster quality and league translation    |   Very high |
| Starting pitcher availability            |   Very high |
| Bullpen coverage                         |   Very high |
| Stage and tie-breaker/mercy-rule context |        High |
| Lineup handedness and power              |        High |
| Defence/catcher quality                  | Medium-high |
| Travel/time-zone/climate                 |      Medium |
| National-team chemistry                  |      Medium |
| Recent domestic/international form       |      Medium |
| Historical head-to-head                  |         Low |

In international baseball, do **not** treat a national team like a club team. The same country can look completely different depending on player availability, MLB club restrictions, pitch limits and tournament timing.

## 12. MLB vs international: key differences to model separately

| Area            | MLB                                         | International                                    |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Sample size     | Huge 162-game season                        | Small tournament samples                         |
| Data quality    | Rich Statcast/tracking                      | Uneven by country/event                          |
| Pitching        | Normal club usage patterns                  | Pitch caps and mandatory rest                    |
| Rosters         | Stable club rosters                         | Availability-dependent national squads           |
| Matchups        | Deep historical data                        | Many unfamiliar matchups                         |
| Rules           | MLB-specific pitch clock, shift/bases rules | Tournament-specific rules and mercy/tie-breakers |
| Motivation      | Season-long playoff race                    | Short-term national tournament pressure          |
| Bullpen         | Managed over series/season                  | Managed under strict caps                        |
| Park factors    | Strong MLB park data                        | Neutral/international venue uncertainty          |
| Prediction risk | Lower uncertainty                           | Higher uncertainty                               |

## 13. MVP build order

### MVP baseball app

Build these first:

* Game metadata and ruleset.
* Starting lineups.
* Probable starting pitchers.
* Bullpen availability.
* Pitch-by-pitch data.
* Batter handedness vs pitcher handedness.
* Batter pitch-type splits.
* Pitcher arsenal and pitch values.
* Park factors.
* Weather and roof status.
* Plate umpire strike-zone profile.
* Recent team/player form.
* Injuries, transactions and rest.

### MLB pro version

Add:

* Full Statcast integration.
* xwOBA/xBA/xSLG.
* Barrel and hard-hit modelling.
* Pitch movement/shape modelling.
* Batter-vs-pitch-shape matchup.
* Bullpen fatigue model.
* Umpire-zone adjustment.
* Fielding Run Value/OAA.
* Park/weather HR model.
* Real-time win probability.

### International pro version

Add:

* League-translation model.
* National-team roster quality model.
* Pitch-limit optimiser.
* Short-tournament bullpen model.
* Mercy-rule and tie-breaker module.
* Unknown-player uncertainty score.
* National-team chemistry/continuity index.
* Cross-league scouting reports.

## 14. Practical app pages

For baseball, I’d build these dashboards:

1. **Game preview page** — starting pitchers, lineups, bullpen fatigue, park/weather, umpire, matchup edge.
2. **Pitcher page** — arsenal, velocity, movement, command, pitch value, fatigue, splits.
3. **Hitter page** — pitch-type performance, xwOBA, barrel %, discipline, handedness splits.
4. **Bullpen page** — availability, leverage arms, fatigue, handedness mix.
5. **Venue page** — park factors, dimensions, roof, weather, HR/run environment.
6. **Umpire page** — zone profile, K/BB effect, run environment.
7. **International tournament page** — pitch limits, roster strength, league translations, tie-breakers.
8. **Live game page** — run expectancy, win probability, leverage, bullpen decision alerts.
9. **Explainability page** — why the model favours a team, total or player prop.

## 15. Final principle

For **MLB**, the app should be built around:

**Statcast quality + starting pitcher + bullpen fatigue + lineup handedness + park/weather + umpire zone.**

For **international baseball**, the app should be built around:

**roster availability + league-strength translation + pitch limits + bullpen depth + tournament rules + neutral-venue uncertainty.**

[13]: https://www.mlb.com/news/world-baseball-classic-rules-rule-modifications-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com "2026 World Baseball Classic rules and rule modifications"
[14]: https://www.nbcmiami.com/mlb/world-baseball-classic-rule-guide/3775957/?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Here is a rule guide for the 2026 World Baseball Classic"


Yes — for **AFL specifically**, I’d make the app less about “who had more disposals” and more about:

**selection + contest + territory + clearance source + turnover source + inside-50 quality + expected score + venue/weather fit.**

AFL is very data-rich, but the key is to store every stat by **quarter, zone, clearance context and possession-chain source**. Champion Data’s AFL warehouse model is a good reference because it dimensions stats by **period, logical zone, physical zone, and whether the stat happened pre- or post-clearance**. ([AFL Data Platform][1]) The AFL’s own glossary also confirms the core Champion Data-style terms you should support, including inside 50s, hit-outs, groundball gets, hardball gets, score assists, spoils, smothers, rebound 50s, tackles and more. ([afl.com.au][2])

## 1. AFL-specific match metadata

| Category            | Fields to capture                                                            |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Match identity      | match ID, round, season, home team, away team, venue, date, local start time |
| Competition context | AFL, AFLW, finals, home-and-away, preseason, Gather Round, neutral venue     |
| Ladder context      | ladder position, percentage, top-four race, finals race, rebuild context     |
| Team sheet          | selected 23, bench/interchange, emergencies, late outs, role changes         |
| Rules version       | season rule set, interchange rules, score review/ARC availability            |
| Match situation     | score, margin, quarter, time remaining, momentum, live win probability       |
| Travel/rest         | rest days, interstate travel, time-zone change, back-to-back travel          |
| Weather/venue       | ground size, roof, rain, wind, temperature, humidity, surface                |
| News context        | injury updates, illness, tribunal, selection hints, coach comments           |

For the 2026 AFL season, version your rules carefully because the AFL confirmed removal of the centre bounce and removal of the substitute, with clubs naming 23 players and five interchange players. ([melbournefc.com.au][3])

### B. Availability, injury and workload

| Area            | Stats/fields                                                                 |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

Use the AFL’s official injury list as a primary source layer because it aggregates injury updates across all 18 clubs. ([afl.com.au][4]) For concussion, the app should store “recognise, remove, refer, review and return” workflow status because the AFL states suspected concussion requires removal and medical assessment, and players must not return the same match if concussion cannot be ruled out. ([afl.com.au][5])

The rules layer should be season-specific because the AFL Laws are explicitly maintained to keep the game exciting, entertaining and safe, and 2026 includes new laws and interpretations. ([Play AFL][6])

## 5. Venue and ground-size data

AFL venue data is unusually important because ground shape and width can materially change team style. For example, AFL venue pages list the MCG at **160m x 141m**, Marvel Stadium at **159.5m x 128.8m**, Optus Stadium at **165m x 130m**, and GMHBA Stadium at **170m x 114m**. ([afl.com.au][7])

| Venue field     | Why it matters                                                    |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Length          | affects long-kick territory, transition chains, key-forward space |
| Width           | affects wing use, switch-kicking, defensive spread                |
| Shape           | narrow, wide, long, pocket depth, straight-line scoring lanes     |
| Roof            | Marvel roof open/closed changes wind/rain variables               |
| Surface         | fast, slippery, heavy, chopped-up, recently resurfaced            |
| Wind            | end-to-end wind, crosswind, swirling wind                         |
| Crowd           | home-ground edge, hostile crowd, expected attendance              |
| Travel          | interstate travel, time zone, short turnaround                    |
| Scoring history | average total points, goal accuracy, behind rate                  |
| Team fit        | whether the team’s style suits the ground dimensions              |

## 6. Weather and time-of-day conditions

| Condition      | Stats/fields                                          |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Time slot      | day, twilight, night, short turnaround                |
| Temperature    | start temp, quarter-by-quarter temp, feels-like temp  |
| Rain           | pre-game rain, live rain, rainfall intensity          |
| Wind           | wind speed, gusts, direction, end-to-end/crosswind    |
| Humidity       | humidity, dew point, greasy-ball risk                 |
| Surface        | dry, wet, heavy, fast, slippery                       |
| Roof           | open, closed, roof-shadow effect                      |
| Sun/glare      | low sun, one-end visibility issue                     |
| Ground wear    | previous events, centre-square wear, goal-square wear |
| Fatigue effect | hot day, high-humidity game, cold/wet repeat efforts  |

Weather should feed directly into projected total points, disposal efficiency, marking volume, contested-ball weighting and goalkicking accuracy.

## 12. AFL vs AFLW/state league adjustments

| Area                  | AFL                                       | AFLW/state league adjustment                               |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Data depth            | Richer stats and more consistent coverage | Expect gaps; store confidence/source quality               |
| Scoring               | Higher scoring baseline                   | Separate scoring distributions                             |
| Venue                 | Major AFL venues                          | More suburban grounds, stronger surface/weather variation  |
| Player availability   | Professional full-time environment        | More external-work/study/travel constraints in lower tiers |
| Role modelling        | Stable tactical roles                     | More role volatility and list changes                      |
| Prediction confidence | Higher with data depth                    | Lower unless lineups/venue/weather are verified            |

The key principle for AFL is:

**Model the game as territory + contest + turnover + forward-entry quality, then adjust for selection, venue, weather, fatigue and rule context.**

Yes. Across **soccer, cricket, AFL and baseball**, there are several universal layers that must be considered beyond the sport-specific stats. These are the things that make the difference between a basic stats app and a serious sports research/prediction app.

The main extra layers are:

**data quality, timing of information, role/context adjustment, opponent strength, injuries/workload, travel, weather, officiating, venue, rule changes, tactical style, uncertainty, model calibration, and post-match learning.**

## 1. Data provenance and source quality

Every stat in your app should have a **source trail**.

Store:

| Field                 | Why it matters                                                                    |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| source name           | AFL, Opta, StatsBomb, Cricsheet, MLB, Statcast, Champion Data, manual notes, etc. |
| source type           | official, provider, journalist, club report, social media, manual tag             |
| timestamp collected   | tells you what was known at prediction time                                       |
| original timestamp    | when the event/news happened                                                      |
| confidence score      | verified, likely, rumour, unconfirmed                                             |
| data version          | important when providers revise stats after review                                |
| manual/automated flag | human-coded data has different error risks                                        |
| update history        | lets you audit corrected or changed records                                       |

This matters because sports data is often revised after the match. For example, assists, pressure acts, tackles, score involvements, errors, xG/xScore, batted-ball metrics or injury statuses can be corrected later. A football data-format paper argues that sports data should be clear, contextualised, complete and include provenance, and it defines match sheet data, event data, tracking data, video footage and match metadata as separate layers. ([arXiv][1])

## 2. Prediction-time availability / no future leakage

This is massive. For each feature, store whether it was available:

| Timing layer        | Example                                            |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| 7 days before match | early injury list, travel, fixture congestion      |
| 48 hours before     | team news, weather forecast, probable lineups      |
| 24 hours before     | squad lists, pitch/venue reports                   |
| 1 hour before       | confirmed lineups, toss, late outs                 |
| live                | score state, momentum, fatigue, substitutions      |
| post-match only     | final stats, official corrections, reviewed events |

Your app should never train a pre-match prediction model using information that only became known after the match started. IBM defines data leakage as a model using information during training that would not be available at prediction time, which can make the model look accurate during testing but fail in real use. ([IBM][2])

For your app, every feature should have:

| Field                  | Example                                   |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `known_at_time`        | 2026-06-13 18:30 AEST                     |
| `prediction_stage`     | pre-lineup, post-lineup, live, post-match |
| `feature_availability` | available / unavailable / estimated       |
| `leakage_risk`         | low / medium / high                       |

## 3. Role-adjusted stats

Raw stats are dangerous unless role-adjusted.

Examples:

| Sport    | Bad raw reading          | Better role-adjusted reading                           |
| -------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Soccer   | defender has low touches | was he a low-block centre-back?                        |
| Cricket  | batter has low average   | did he bat at No. 6 in death-over situations?          |
| AFL      | player has few disposals | was he a lockdown defender or pressure forward?        |
| Baseball | hitter has low average   | was he facing elite lefties in pitcher-friendly parks? |

Store role-specific expectations:

| Universal field            | Examples                                                          |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| role at selection          | opener, winger, ruck, closer                                      |
| role in match              | actual role, changed role, emergency role                         |
| expected usage             | minutes, overs, innings, at-bats, centre-bounce attendances       |
| role difficulty            | opponent quality, defensive assignment, pitch/ground/park context |
| role output above expected | player’s production vs role baseline                              |

This prevents your app from overrating high-volume players and underrating high-value role players.

## 4. Opponent-strength adjustment

Always adjust form and stats by **quality of opposition**.

Store:

| Field                       | Why it matters                                          |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| opponent rating             | Elo/SPI/power rating/ladder rating                      |
| opponent recent form        | last 5/10/20 adjusted results                           |
| opponent style              | high press, spin-heavy, clearance-heavy, fastball-heavy |
| opponent defensive strength | quality of resistance faced                             |
| opponent injury status      | whether the opponent was full strength                  |
| opponent venue fit          | whether opponent was advantaged/disadvantaged by venue  |
| opponent rest/travel        | fatigue or schedule edge                                |

Example: a cricket team scoring 190 against an elite attack on a slow pitch is not the same as scoring 190 against a weak attack on a flat pitch. An AFL team winning clearances against a bottom midfield is not the same as winning clearances against Melbourne, Brisbane, Collingwood, Sydney, etc.

## 5. Strength of schedule and fixture difficulty

Every sport needs a strength-of-schedule layer.

Track:

| Field                        | Examples                                               |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| recent opponent difficulty   | average rating of last 5/10 opponents                  |
| upcoming opponent difficulty | next 3/5 fixtures                                      |
| travel density               | away trips, international trips, interstate travel     |
| fixture congestion           | matches in 7/14/30 days                                |
| rest differential            | your rest days minus opponent rest days                |
| schedule trap                | lookahead game, rivalry next, final next, cup tie next |

This is especially important for AFL and soccer because fatigue and travel affect pressing, defensive transition, running capacity and late-game performance. It also matters in MLB because bullpen usage and travel can heavily affect game-to-game outcomes.

## 6. Travel, jet lag and recovery

Travel should not be a simple “home/away” flag. Store it properly.

| Field                | Why it matters                       |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| kilometres travelled | fatigue/load                         |
| time zones crossed   | circadian rhythm                     |
| days since arrival   | adaptation                           |
| direction of travel  | eastward travel is often harder      |
| travel sequence      | road trip game 1 vs game 6           |
| sleep disruption     | late arrival, early start            |
| short break          | reduced recovery                     |
| previous venue       | weather/surface/time-zone transition |

A 2021 review on travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes notes that travel can increase subjective burden and may influence performance, illness and injury risk. ([PMC][3])

## 7. Workload, fatigue and injury-risk context

Across all sports, you should track workload separately from form.

| Universal workload field | Soccer          | Cricket                  | AFL                    | Baseball               |
| ------------------------ | --------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------- | ---------------------- |
| recent minutes/load      | minutes played  | overs bowled/balls faced | time on ground/GPS     | pitches thrown/innings |
| high-intensity work      | sprints         | fast-bowling spells      | high-speed running     | velocity/drop-off      |
| recovery                 | rest days       | days since spell         | short break            | days since outing      |
| injury history           | hamstring/groin | back/side strain         | concussion/soft tissue | elbow/shoulder         |
| return status            | minutes cap     | bowling restriction      | managed minutes        | pitch count            |

Use workload as a **risk signal**, not as a simple rule. Acute:chronic workload ratio research notes that workload monitoring is useful but has limitations and can be affected by confounding and sparse data. ([arXiv][4])

## 8. Weather, climate and environment

Weather should be stored as a **time series**, not one value.

| Weather field         | Why it matters                                                    |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| temperature           | fatigue, ball movement, scoring conditions                        |
| humidity              | heat stress, dew, grip                                            |
| rain                  | surface, ball handling, postponement/interruption                 |
| wind speed/direction  | AFL goalkicking, baseball HR carry, soccer crosses, cricket swing |
| cloud cover           | cricket swing, visibility                                         |
| dew point             | cricket wet ball, evening conditions                              |
| air pressure/altitude | baseball ball carry, endurance                                    |
| WBGT                  | heat stress risk                                                  |
| surface condition     | slippery, heavy, fast, dry, cracked                               |
| roof status           | MLB/AFL venues with roofs                                         |

For heat, wet-bulb globe temperature is especially useful because consensus heat recommendations often use WBGT to guide whether events should be modified, delayed or cancelled. ([PMC][5])

## 9. Venue-specific effects

Your app should have a full venue model.

| Venue field         | Soccer             | Cricket             | AFL                      | Baseball              |
| ------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------------- |
| dimensions          | pitch size         | boundary size       | oval length/width        | park dimensions       |
| surface             | grass/artificial   | pitch/outfield      | grass, roof, ground size | grass/turf            |
| scoring history     | goals              | average score/chase | total points/xScore      | park factor           |
| weather sensitivity | rain/wind          | dew/swing/spin      | wind/rain/roof           | wind/altitude         |
| home advantage      | crowd/travel       | pitch familiarity   | ground familiarity       | batting backdrop/park |
| tactical fit        | pressing/wide play | spin/pace           | corridor/wide switch     | HR/pitcher park       |

Venue fit is more important than most people think. A team can be strong overall but poorly suited to a specific ground, pitch, park or weather profile.

## 10. Official/referee/umpire profile

Officials are not noise. They change the environment.

| Official layer | Soccer         | Cricket              | AFL                 | Baseball         |
| -------------- | -------------- | -------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------- |
| strictness     | cards/fouls    | wides/no-balls       | free kicks/50m      | strike zone      |
| pace of game   | stoppages      | light/rain decisions | ball-ups/free kicks | pitch clock/zone |
| discipline     | reds/cards     | code of conduct      | reports/MRO         | ejections        |
| review system  | VAR            | DRS                  | ARC/score review    | replay           |
| style fit      | pressing teams | LBW/spin             | contested teams     | control pitchers |

Store officials by **rate tendencies**, not just names.

## 11. Rule changes and competition-specific rules

Rules must be versioned by season and competition.

| Rule type                | Examples                                                      |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| substitution/interchange | soccer subs, AFL sub/interchange, cricket impact/replacements |
| timing                   | pitch clock, stoppage time, over rates                        |
| review systems           | VAR, DRS, ARC, replay                                         |
| tournament rules         | DLS, Super Over, extra time, penalties, pitch limits          |
| equipment rules          | ball type, bat rules, pitch dimensions                        |
| disciplinary rules       | suspensions, yellow-card accumulation, MRO/tribunal           |
| scoring/tiebreakers      | NRR, percentage, goal difference, head-to-head                |

If the app compares historical seasons, rule changes must be stored or your model will learn from a different environment.

## 12. Lineup/selection uncertainty

Before confirmed teams, your app should not treat expected lineups as facts.

Store:

| Field                        | Example                                     |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| expected starter probability | 80% likely to start                         |
| confirmed starter            | true/false                                  |
| role probability             | 60% midfield, 30% forward, 10% sub/bench    |
| minutes/usage projection     | expected minutes, overs, pitches, rotations |
| late-out risk                | low/medium/high                             |
| replacement quality          | starter vs backup drop-off                  |
| bench/sub impact             | attacking/defensive depth                   |

This is critical because prediction quality often changes dramatically once final teams are known.

## 13. Tactical and style matchup

Every team should have a style profile.

| Style category       | Examples                                                    |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| tempo                | fast/slow, direct/controlled                                |
| pressure             | high press, forward-half pressure, bowling pressure         |
| territory            | field position, inside 50s, final-third entries             |
| transition           | counterattack, turnover scoring, defensive transition       |
| set pieces/stoppages | corners, centre bounces, clearances, dead-ball plays        |
| personnel style      | tall/short, pace/spin, left/right, power/contact            |
| risk tolerance       | aggressive ball movement, conservative possession           |
| coaching style       | early subs, bullpen hook, rotation pattern, defensive setup |

The model should ask: **does Team A’s strength attack Team B’s weakness?** Not just “who is better overall?”

## 14. Match-state context

A stat is not the same in every game state.

Track all stats by state:

| State                | Why it matters             |
| -------------------- | -------------------------- |
| leading              | teams become conservative  |
| trailing             | teams take more risks      |
| tied                 | balanced decision-making   |
| early game           | planned tactics            |
| late game            | fatigue/clutch/bench depth |
| high leverage        | pressure decisions         |
| garbage time         | stats can mislead          |
| weather interruption | rhythm changes             |
| injury during match  | role changes               |

Examples:

* Soccer shots while trailing may inflate attack stats.
* Cricket death-over strike rate depends on wickets in hand.
* AFL disposals while chasing can be low-quality.
* Baseball bullpen choices depend heavily on score and inning.

## 15. Garbage-time and score-effects adjustment

Do not treat all stats equally.

| Sport    | Garbage-time issue                                      |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Soccer   | late shots when opponent is protecting a lead           |
| Cricket  | chasing impossible target or dead-rubber overs          |
| AFL      | junk-time goals/disposals in a blowout                  |
| Baseball | position players pitching, low-leverage bullpen innings |

Create fields:

| Field                | Meaning                               |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| leverage level       | low/medium/high                       |
| game competitiveness | live contest/blowout/dead rubber      |
| score effect         | trailing pressure, leading protection |
| garbage-time flag    | yes/no                                |
| adjusted stat weight | full/partial/low                      |

## 16. Market consensus and odds movement — optional but useful

Even if your app is not a betting app, market prices can be useful as a **benchmark**, not as the final answer.

Track:

| Field                | Use                                       |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| opening line         | early market expectation                  |
| closing line         | final market consensus                    |
| line movement        | injury/news/weather reaction              |
| implied probability  | baseline comparison                       |
| bookmaker margin     | vig/overround                             |
| market disagreement  | sharp vs public split if available        |
| model edge vs market | your probability minus market probability |

If the app is used for probability decisions, calibration matters more than just “accuracy”. A sports betting model-selection paper found that selecting models based on calibration rather than raw accuracy produced better betting outcomes in its NBA experiments. ([arXiv][6]) Scikit-learn’s calibration documentation also explains that for classification, predicted probabilities should represent confidence in the class, and some models give poor probability estimates unless calibrated. ([Scikit-learn][7])

## 17. News and sentiment layer

Track news, but classify it carefully.

| News type             | Importance  |
| --------------------- | ----------- |
| confirmed injury      | very high   |
| confirmed lineup      | very high   |
| coach tactical quote  | medium-high |
| training absence      | medium-high |
| illness outbreak      | high        |
| internal unrest       | medium      |
| transfer/trade rumour | low-medium  |
| fan sentiment         | low         |
| media hype            | usually low |

Store:

| Field                 | Example                                                   |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| source credibility    | club > league > reliable journalist > social media rumour |
| confirmed/unconfirmed | official vs rumour                                        |
| affected player/team  | ID-linked                                                 |
| expected impact       | role, availability, morale, tactics                       |
| timestamp             | when the news became public                               |
| model usage           | included/excluded                                         |

## 18. Data-confidence scoring

Not every feature deserves the same trust.

| Confidence level | Example                 |
| ---------------- | ----------------------- |
| 1.00             | official final score    |
| 0.95             | official team sheet     |
| 0.90             | official injury list    |
| 0.80             | reputable beat reporter |
| 0.65             | coach hint              |
| 0.50             | model-estimated lineup  |
| 0.30             | fan/social rumour       |

Use confidence scores in your model and in the UI. For example: “Team X is favoured, but confidence is reduced because the lineup is unconfirmed and weather is unstable.”

## 19. Model evaluation and backtesting

Your app should not only predict — it should learn.

Track:

| Evaluation metric      | Purpose                                        |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| accuracy               | did the winner/outcome hit?                    |
| log loss               | probability quality                            |
| Brier score            | probability forecast error                     |
| calibration curve      | whether 70% predictions actually hit about 70% |
| ROI/CLV                | only if betting use case                       |
| mean absolute error    | margin/score projection                        |
| residual analysis      | where model was wrong                          |
| feature attribution    | why model predicted something                  |
| time-split backtesting | avoids future leakage                          |

Reliability diagrams are a standard way to assess calibration by comparing predicted probabilities with observed frequencies. ([arXiv][8])

## 20. Post-match learning loop

After each event, store:

| Post-match field          | Purpose                                    |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| predicted outcome         | what model said                            |
| actual outcome            | what happened                              |
| prediction timestamp      | pre-lineup/post-lineup/live                |
| biggest missed assumption | injury, weather, lineup, tactics, variance |
| winning features          | what mattered                              |
| misleading features       | what looked important but wasn’t           |
| update recommendation     | model weight change or data gap            |
| human note                | analyst explanation                        |

This is especially useful for your style of research because you often compare ranked options. The app should show **why the ranking was right or wrong**, not just whether it hit.

## 21. Universal “must-have” feature table

If you want one master checklist across soccer, cricket, AFL and baseball, use this:

| Feature group                | Must capture? | Why                                                |
| ---------------------------- | ------------: | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Confirmed lineup/team sheet  |           Yes | biggest pre-match swing factor                     |
| Availability/injuries        |           Yes | changes roles, rotations and quality               |
| Recent form by role          |           Yes | raw form is not enough                             |
| Opponent-adjusted stats      |           Yes | prevents weak-schedule bias                        |
| Venue/ground/park/pitch      |           Yes | changes scoring environment                        |
| Weather/time of day          |           Yes | affects skill execution and fatigue                |
| Officials                    |           Yes | changes foul/card/free-kick/strike/DRS environment |
| Rest/travel/fatigue          |           Yes | changes physical output                            |
| Tactical/style matchup       |           Yes | explains why underdogs can match up well           |
| Match context/stakes         |           Yes | changes risk-taking and selection                  |
| Rule version                 |           Yes | prevents historical comparison errors              |
| Market/odds benchmark        |      Optional | useful as consensus benchmark                      |
| Data provenance              |           Yes | prevents bad-source/hallucination errors           |
| Prediction-time availability |           Yes | prevents future leakage                            |
| Calibration/backtesting      |           Yes | tells if probabilities are trustworthy             |
| Uncertainty/confidence       |           Yes | avoids overconfident bad predictions               |

Across every sport, I’d include these shared tables:

## 23. Biggest mistakes to avoid

The main ones:

1. **Using post-match data in pre-match models.**
2. **Not separating confirmed vs predicted lineups.**
3. **Overvaluing recent wins/losses.**
4. **Ignoring opponent strength.**
5. **Ignoring venue/weather/rules.**
6. **Treating all player roles equally.**
7. **Using one model across different formats/rulesets.**
8. **Failing to version data and model outputs.**
9. **Reporting a prediction without confidence or uncertainty.**
10. **Not doing post-match review and model calibration.**

## Final app principle

For all these sports, your app should be built around this chain:

**verified source → timestamped data → role/context adjustment → matchup model → probability output → confidence score → post-match review.**

That structure will help you avoid hallucinated analysis, stale stats, misleading form, and overconfident predictions.

[1]: https://arxiv.org/html/2505.15820v1?utm_source=chatgpt.com "a Standardized Format for Match-Data in Football (Soccer)"
[2]: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/data-leakage-machine-learning?utm_source=chatgpt.com "What is Data Leakage in Machine Learning?"
[3]: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8279034/?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes - PMC - NIH"
[4]: https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05326?utm_source=chatgpt.com "The acute:chronic workload ratio: challenges and prospects for improvement"
[5]: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4602249/?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Consensus recommendations on training and competing in ..."
[6]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06021?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Machine learning for sports betting: should model selection be based on accuracy or calibration?"
[7]: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com "1.16. Probability calibration"
[8]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Evaluating probabilistic classifiers: Reliability diagrams and score decompositions revisited"


Correct — for your app, you should separate **pre-game prediction inputs** from **live/in-game stats** and **post-game review stats**.

The rule should be:

**Only use information that was knowable before the game started.**
Historical stats are fine, but they must be calculated only from matches completed **before your data cutoff**. Do not let live stats, final score, post-match xG/xScore, post-match injuries, or revised event data leak into a pre-game model.

A recent leakage-detection paper defines leakage as contamination with information unavailable at baseline, which is exactly the issue you need to avoid in pre-game sports modelling. ([arXiv][1])

## 1. Pre-game data snapshots

Your app should save multiple snapshots before each match.

| Snapshot          | What it should contain                                                              |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| T-7 days          | fixture, venue, early injury list, travel/rest, ladder/table context                |
| T-48 hours        | weather forecast, likely lineups, availability news, form, tactical notes           |
| T-24 hours        | updated squad/team news, pitch/venue reports, referee/umpire info                   |
| T-3 hours         | late injury rumours, weather update, confirmed/probable lineups where available     |
| T-1 hour          | confirmed lineups/team sheets, bench/subs, late outs                                |
| Just before start | final pre-game state: toss in cricket, roof/weather, lineup confirmation, officials |

Every prediction should be linked to a specific `prediction_snapshot_id`.

## 2. Core pre-game fields across every sport

| Feature group                | Must collect pre-game? | Why it matters                                         |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------: | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Fixture details              |                    Yes | Date, venue, home/away, competition, stage             |
| Confirmed/probable lineup    |                    Yes | Biggest late swing factor                              |
| Injury/availability status   |                    Yes | Changes role quality and rotations                     |
| Suspension/discipline status |                    Yes | Removes key players or changes aggression              |
| Recent form                  |                    Yes | Use last 5/10/15/20, but opponent-adjusted             |
| Season baseline              |                    Yes | Prevents overreacting to small samples                 |
| Home/away split              |                    Yes | Venue and travel impact                                |
| Opponent strength            |                    Yes | Adjusts raw form for schedule difficulty               |
| Venue profile                |                    Yes | Ground/pitch/park/stadium changes scoring              |
| Weather forecast             |                    Yes | Affects scoring, fatigue, handling, ball movement      |
| Officials                    |                    Yes | Cards, free kicks, strike zone, DRS, reviews           |
| Rest/travel                  |                    Yes | Fatigue and preparation edge                           |
| Tactical/style matchup       |                    Yes | Strength-vs-weakness analysis                          |
| Motivation/context           |                    Yes | Finals, relegation, ladder, qualification, dead rubber |
| Market line                  |               Optional | Useful as benchmark only, not primary reason           |
| Source confidence            |                    Yes | Separates official fact from rumour                    |
| Data cutoff                  |                    Yes | Prevents future leakage                                |

## 3. Universal pre-game schema

Every stat or feature should have these fields:

| Field                    | Example                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `match_id`               | unique fixture ID                                      |
| `sport`                  | soccer, cricket, AFL, baseball                         |
| `feature_name`           | expected lineup strength                               |
| `feature_value`          | 0.82                                                   |
| `raw_value`              | “Player X out, Player Y starts”                        |
| `source`                 | official league, team site, stats provider, journalist |
| `source_tier`            | official / provider / journalist / rumour              |
| `known_at_time`          | 2026-06-13 18:30 AEST                                  |
| `prediction_cutoff`      | T-1 hour                                               |
| `confirmed_status`       | confirmed / projected / doubtful / unknown             |
| `confidence_score`       | 0.95 official, 0.70 reliable reporter, etc.            |
| `leakage_risk`           | low / medium / high                                    |
| `sport_specific_context` | toss, roof, umpire, pitch, weather, team sheet         |

## 4. What must **not** be used in pre-game models

Do not use:

| Do not use                              | Why                                    |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Final score                             | post-game leakage                      |
| In-game xG/xScore                       | not known pre-game                     |
| Live possession/territory               | not known pre-game                     |
| Actual substitution pattern             | only known after match starts          |
| In-game injury/removal                  | not known pre-game                     |
| Post-match official stat corrections    | not available at prediction time       |
| Actual weather during match             | use forecast only for pre-game         |
| Actual toss outcome before it happens   | cricket only becomes usable after toss |
| Actual starting lineup before confirmed | store as projected, not confirmed      |

For weather, use **forecast data** for pre-game predictions and historical weather only for backtesting. Open-Meteo, for example, separates forecast APIs from historical/reanalysis weather datasets, which is the type of distinction your database should preserve. ([Open-Meteo][2])

## 5. Pre-game soccer stats

### Must-have soccer pre-game inputs

| Category      | Pre-game stats/information                                               |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Fixture       | competition, round, home/away, neutral venue, kickoff time               |
| Table context | league position, points need, relegation/title/top-four context          |
| Lineups       | confirmed XI, projected XI, bench strength, formation                    |
| Availability  | injuries, suspensions, illness, international duty, minutes restrictions |
| Recent form   | last 5/10/15/20 results, goals, xG, xGA, clean sheets                    |
| Home/away     | home xG/xGA, away xG/xGA, home scoring/conceding                         |
| Attack        | goals, xG, shots, shots on target, big chances, set-piece threat         |
| Defence       | xGA, shots conceded, box shots conceded, clean sheets                    |
| Goalkeeper    | save %, goals prevented, recent errors, availability                     |
| Style         | possession, pressing, directness, counterattack, set-piece reliance      |
| Matchup       | fullback vs winger, striker vs centre-backs, midfield control            |
| Referee       | cards per game, fouls, penalties, VAR tendency                           |
| Venue         | pitch size, surface, home crowd, travel                                  |
| Weather       | rain, wind, temperature, surface condition                               |

For data design, StatsBomb open data is a useful structural reference because it separates competitions, matches, events, lineups and 360 data by match ID. ([GitHub][3])

## 6. Pre-game cricket stats

Champion Data’s AFL platform gives access to AFL match statistics, fixtures, squads and player data, and the AFL glossary defines the core stats used in AFL analysis such as inside 50s, hit-outs, groundball gets, spoils and rebound 50s. ([AFL Data Platform][5])

Venue dimensions should be a proper pre-game feature. For example, Optus Stadium lists AFL field dimensions of **165m x 130m**, and its fact sheet notes this is closely aligned with the MCG’s **160m x 141m** field dimensions. ([afl.com.au][6])

MLB/Statcast data is especially useful here because Statcast supports expected statistics and park-factor modelling. Statcast park factors set **100 as average** and compare player outcomes in a park versus the same players’ outcomes in other parks, controlled by handedness. ([baseballsavant.com][7])
